quote: The inferior colliculus (IC) is the primary auditory midbrain structure that forms a major convergence zone within the auditory system, receiving obligatory bottom-up connections from the brainstem auditory structures, and direct corticofugal feedback connections from auditory cortex.

value: Because BOLD reports synaptic input and local-circuit activity more than output spiking, the measured map tracks the interdigitated tonotopy of cochlear-nucleus afferents rather than the smooth map of IC neurons, producing patches.
quote: Accordingly, our results may more closely reflect the patchy, somewhat interdigitated tonotopic organization of bottom-up neuronal inputs to IC from the cochlear nucleus, as reported by anterograde labeling studies (Oliver and Morest, 1984 ; Hofstetter and Ehret, 1992 ; Loftus et al., 2008 ).

value: At 3 T half the BOLD signal is intravascular, so tissue near large draining veins yields strong contrast and tissue away from them yields little, imposing a vascular patch pattern on the frequency map.
quote: If so, the observed patchy structure may reflect stronger contrast from regions of IC where there are larger concentrations of draining veins, while little contrast is observed in other regions.

value: Attentive auditory tasks bias processing to the left hemisphere, and largely ipsilateral corticocollicular feedback carries that bias down to the colliculus, yielding stronger left-IC gradients.
quote: Auditory tasks that require attentive processing are known to show a left-hemispheric bias (Bryden et al., 1983 ) and can modulate IC activity via corticocollicular connections (Rinne et al., 2007 , 2008 ).

value: Each voxel averages millions of neurons of mixed frequency preference, so within-voxel heterogeneity broadens the apparent tuning and compresses the measured gradient range.
quote: Each voxel encompasses a volume of ∼1.7 μL containing several million neurons, so some heterogeneity of response can be expected.

value: sparse sampling puts the acquisition in the flat top of the BOLD response and in a quiet gap, so scanner noise does not drive the measurement
quote: In sparse-sampling designs, one attempts to sample the hyperoxic peak of the BOLD response evoked by preceding stimulus, then allocate a sufficient delay to allow that response to decay away before the next sample is obtained. Moreover, the delay is adjusted so that the nuisance response from the scanner-acquisition noise is minimized

value: three-shot spiral acquisition acts as a temporal anti-aliasing filter against cardiac and respiratory noise, avoiding the need for gating
quote: The use of the three-shot spiral acquisition acts as a temporal anti-aliasing filter that substantially reduces high-frequency physiological nuisance effects, particularly cardiac pulsations. In single-shot acquisition, each fMRI slice is acquired very quickly (∼20–30 ms) compared to hemodynamic time scales, but the samples are widely spaced (e.g., 2–3 s). This results in aliasing of high-frequency fluctuations driven by cardiac pulse (>1 Hz) and respiration (∼0.25 Hz). In our multi-shot imaging, acquisition is now distributed over multiple brief sampling periods separated by the relatively short TR = 1 s. This preparation implements a low-pass filter upon the data.

value: the external cortex is identified and discarded before the depth analysis because tonotopy is not a feature of it
quote: Since tonotopy is not a feature of the external cortex of the IC, this region is ignored in the subsequent depth analysis.

value: an adaptive staircase on a frequency-discrimination task holds attention roughly constant throughout scanning
quote: During stimulus periods, the frequency difference, typically 3–8%, between the two sounds was adjusted in real time using a pair of randomly interleaved two-up, one-down staircases. After each run, the subject’s current frequency-discrimination threshold value was estimated as the average frequency difference over the latter half of the trials in that run. Frequency difference for the next run was then initialized to a value 30% greater than this estimate. This creates a stable pattern of performance in which subjects perform very well on the task at the start of each run, and then steadily return to their threshold value

value: High-resolution 3 T fMRI resolves a depth tonotopy in human inferior colliculus, with superficial tissue preferring low frequencies and deeper tissue high frequencies, in both ICs of every subject.
quote: We observed significant tonotopy in the depth of IC tissue, with superficial layers showing greater preference to low frequencies and deeper layers to high frequencies.

value: Unlike the smooth gradients reported at 4.7 T and 7 T, the frequency map measured here is spatially patchy rather than continuous.
quote: In contrast to these studies, the detailed spatial structure of our preferred-frequency measurements shows a patchy character.

value: Re-running the whole analysis on data blurred with a 2-mm kernel reproduced the same patchy layout, so the patchiness is signal rather than thermal noise.
quote: This result indicates that the observed patchiness is a real feature of the data, and not the consequence of random noise.

value: Depth gradients were stronger and covered more tissue in the left colliculus than the right.
quote: Gradients were typically stronger and more extensive on the left colliculus then on the right.

value: Frequency tuning is broadest in the middle of the stimulus range: tuning widths at mid frequencies exceed those at the low and high ends by about 40%, giving an inverted-U profile.
quote: On average, tuning widths are about 40% broader at intermediate frequencies than they are at the lower and higher ends of the stimulus frequency band.

value: Paradoxically the very center of the colliculus, where a clean depth tonotopy was expected, showed the weakest gradients.
quote: In particular, we tend to observe weaker tonotopic depth gradients in the very center of the IC, an area expected to have a clearly organized depth tonotopy.

value: significant tonotopic depth gradients were found in both ICs of all four subjects
quote: Significant ( p < 0.05) patches of tonotopic representation with depth were evident in all subjects (Figure 5 ). Significant gradients varied from 0.3 to 1.2 octaves/mm.

value: superficial tissue prefers low frequencies and deeper tissue high frequencies

However, the blurring tends to reduce the absolute magnitude of the depth gradients, and increases the area of reversed gradients observed at the margins of the colliculi.
